description.value: The study used fMRI and multivariate pattern classification to decode the direction of auditory motion from dorsal occipito-temporal activation patterns in four blind human participants, with static auditory stimuli and posterior parietal cortex as controls.

spans.text: Here we used fMRI and multivariate pattern classification to demonstrate that the direction in which a sound is moving can be reliably decoded from dorsal occipito-temporal activation in the blind.

description.value: Observational, repeated-measures neuroimaging study of four blind male volunteers who completed an auditory motion paradigm during eight fMRI runs.

spans.text: After being positioned within the bore of the magnet, subjects completed eight experimental runs with concurrent fMRI recording.
A 2 × 2 factorial design with factors condition (moving vs. static) and direction (leftward vs. rightward) served to identify neural ensembles coding for the direction of auditory motion.

spans.text: In the dorsal occipito-temporal ROI, decoding of the two motion directions exceeded chance performance in each of the four participants (Fig. 3).

spans.text: We then trained a logistic regression classifier and evaluated its performance by predicting stimulus direction on each fMRI volume in the independent test data, using an eight-fold crossvalidation.

Decoding the direction of auditory motion in blind humans

description.value: Participants listened to blocks of moving or static broadband noise stimuli presented through headphones. Moving sounds traveled leftward or rightward, and participants detected deviant stimulus speed or duration with a button press.

spans.text: Subjects listened to blocks of moving and static stimuli (Fig. 1, block duration: 19s), and within each block, five stimuli were presented in rapid succession (stimulus duration: 3 s, ISI: 1 s).

description.value: Broadband noise moving from right to left.
Broadband noise moving from left to right.

spans.text: Motion in the opposite direction (left-to-right) was simulated by reversing the recording channels.

description.value: Static control stimulus preserving the beginning and ending spatial positions of the leftward motion stimulus but lacking the intervening motion component.
Static control stimulus preserving the beginning and ending spatial positions of the rightward motion stimulus but lacking the intervening motion component.

The recordings were downsampled to 44.1 kHz, and presented using Vizard 3.0 (WorldViz, Santa Barbara, CA).

instructions.value: Participants were instructed to attend to the speed or duration of the stimuli and press a button as quickly as possible upon detecting the deviant stimulus; direction was irrelevant.

spans.text: Subjects were instructed to press a button on a keypad with the right index finger as quickly as possible upon detecting the deviant stimulus.

stimuli.value: Binaurally recorded broadband noise from a moving loudspeaker, with moving and static control stimuli.

spans.text: The sound source was a small full-range loudspeaker (Fostex model FF85K 3-inch driver mounted in a 0.7-l sealed enclosure) emitting a broadband noise signal (0.1–20 kHz, 3 s duration).
Subjects were instructed to press a button on a keypad with the right index finger as quickly as possible upon detecting the deviant stimulus.

Deviant stimuli were detected with near-perfect accuracy (> 95%) in all four conditions, and a repeated measures ANOVA did not reveal any differences between moving and static stimuli (accuracy: p = 0.49, reaction times: p = 0.13).
dorsal occipito-temporal ROI
For each subject we sought to define a region of interest (ROI) that was presumed to encompass the hMT+ complex.
We then defined an occipito-temporal region in each participant as the cluster of contiguous voxels near the intersection of the lateral occipital sulcus and the inferior temporal sulcus.

description.value: For each participant, a cluster of contiguous voxels near the intersection of the lateral occipital sulcus and inferior temporal sulcus showing stronger BOLD responses to moving than static sounds, thresholded at p < 0.01 uncorrected; left and right hemispheres were combined.

spans.text: We then defined an occipito-temporal region in each participant as the cluster of contiguous voxels near the intersection of the lateral occipital sulcus and the inferior temporal sulcus.

To test whether or not any potential classification results were specific to the occipito-temporal ROI, we defined a control ROI that also showed sensitivity to auditory motion but where we did not expect directional tuning.

Therefore, we applied the same statistical test to identify clusters of contiguous voxels in posterior parietal cortex that showed stronger BOLD responses for moving vs. static sounds, collapsed across both directions.

description.value: Clusters of contiguous voxels in posterior parietal cortex showing stronger BOLD responses to moving than static sounds, collapsed across directions; left and right hemispheres were combined.

description.value: Functional images were realigned, minimally smoothed for multivariate classification, detrended, temporally filtered, and normalized within run. Univariate analyses used a 6-mm isotropic smoothing kernel.

spans.text: For the univariate analyses, we first realigned all volumes to the first volume in the time series to correct for spatial displacements within and across runs, using SPM8 (Wellcome Department of Imaging Neuroscience, London, UK).
using SPM8 (Wellcome Department of Imaging Neuroscience, London, UK).
Next, we detrended the images to remove linear trends and applied low and high-pass filtering to increase signal-to-noise ratio.
Data samples used for decoding were created by minimally smoothing the realigned images with a 3 mm full-width at half-maximum isotropic Gaussian kernel.
Next, we performed a standard univariate statistical analysis with a general linear model as implemented in SPM8.
